sections.html:
• Scientific name: Sturisomatichthys leightoni (Regan, 1912)
  • Family: Loricariidae
  • Common names: Dwarf Royal Twig Catfish; Leightons Störwels (Germany)
  • Synonym: Oxyloricaria leightoni
  • Size: 180 mm (7.1") SL
  • Temperature: 20.0–24.0°C (68–75.2°F)
  • Breeding: unreported

Until recently, two genera of closely related whiptail catfish were distinguished according to anatomical features: the relatively short-nosed Sturisomatichthys with four described species and the relatively long-nosed Sturisoma with over 15 species. All species are popular aquarium fish because they are attractive and easy to breed.

In well acclimatized animals one can recognize in S. sp. Colombia1 numerous spots and worm lines on the front body, which are missing in S. leightoni. Unfortunately these colour features fade to unrecognizability in stressed animals. The species S. guaitipan from the upper and middle Rio Magdalena in Colombia, newly described in December 2019, is very similar to S. sp. Colombia1, but the unique feature for S. guaitipan is that it has only 10 branched fin rays in the caudal fin, while both animals photographed for this post have 12 branched rays in the caudal fin.
South America: Upper Magdalena and Cauca River basins, Colombia Caribbean Rivers. Type locality: Honda, Colombia, elevation 300-400 feet.
South America: Upper Magdalena and Cauca River basins, Colombia. Type locality: Honda, Colombia, 300–400 ft.
Peaceful species which likes a spacious aquarium with cooler water temperatures of between 20–24°C and clean, soft and slightly acidic water.
Spinach, peas, algae disks, tablet foods and sunken flake foods.
The males develop pronounced tufts of odontodes on either side of the head and the first dorsal ray and the upper and lower caudal fin rays are elongated.
Breeding: unreported. There are 2 breeding reports on the site.

Unlike most other loricariid catfish they do not breed in caves, but lay their eggs openly (usually on one of the vertical aquarium panes). After spawning the male guards the clutch until the young hatch.

This species sports a golden sheen on the sides of the head and is one of the smallest in the genus. The work carried out by Covain et al. 2016 confines the genus Sturisoma to east of the Andes (cis-Andean), and the genus Sturisomatichthys to the west of the Andes (trans-Andean).

Etymology: the specific name leightoni honours British soldier Bryan Leighton (1868–1919), who "presented" the holotype to the British Museum (Natural History).

IUCN Red List: the species has a relatively wide range. Although data are lacking on its population size and trend or the threats affecting it, it appears to be relatively common. It is listed as Least Concern.

As a rule of thumb, Sturisomatichthys remain smaller (10-12 cm), while Sturisoma can be expected to reach 15-30 cm (depending on the species). A recent study by Alejandro Londoño-Burbano and Roberto E. Reis showed that all species from Colombia, Venezuela and Panama are so closely related that they belong to the same genus, Sturisomatichthys, while the species from the entire Amazon basin and further south to Paraguay remain in Sturisoma.
